unit.title: Perform head, neck and shoulder massage

summary: This unit teaches you to give a safe, relaxing seated head, neck and shoulder massage: prepare the room, yourself and the client, consult and check for contra-indications, choose a massage medium, and use effleurage, petrissage, friction, tapotement and vibration with the right pressure. You will learn the bones, muscles and vessels you work over, the areas to avoid, how to adapt the massage for different clients, and how to give aftercare, clean up and keep records.

blocks.p: This unit covers a complete seated head, neck and shoulder massage, from the moment you greet the client to the moment you write up her record card. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. A short massage like this is offered in salons, spas, at wellness days in offices and at events. It is also the base for the scalp and shoulder massage you give during other services.

A good massage relaxes the client, eases tight muscles and leaves her feeling calm. A careless one can hurt her, make an illness or injury worse, or pass on an infection. That is why this unit is about **safety, judgement and communication** as much as hand movements. You are not a doctor or a physiotherapist: you do not diagnose, you do not claim to cure anything, and you refer clients when you are not sure.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks at the Centre. In the practical tasks you give a full seated massage with a consultation, and you also show your knowledge of the bones and muscles, decide whether to massage, adapt or refer for different clients, and give a dry massage over clothing. The assessor watches your consultation, hygiene, pressure, posture and records, not only your hands.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only shoulders, the back of the head and your hands. Never photograph a model's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Preparing the room, yourself and the client

blocks.p: Most of a good massage is decided before you touch the client. A calm, clean, well-prepared setting helps her relax, and it keeps both of you safe.

head: Part of the set-up
What to do
Why
rows: Temperature and air
Comfortably warm; fresh air from a window or air conditioning
A fan must not blow directly on the client
Muscles tighten in the cold. A draught on a bare neck can chill the client and spoil the massage.
Noise and privacy
Quiet, with a screen or door closed
Soft, calm music if the client likes it
She must feel safe enough to relax and to talk about her health.
Light
Soft but bright enough for you to see the skin and scalp
You must be able to see cuts, rashes and bruises.
The chair
Sturdy, with an upright back and no wheels that roll
Wiped with disinfectant and covered with a clean towel
Or a massage chair with a face rest, wiped clean
A chair that moves or tips is a danger. The next client must meet a clean chair.
Supplies within reach
Clean towels and a gown or wrap, tissues
Medium in a clean bowl, with a spatula for cream
Water and cups; consultation form and pen; clock or timer
Hair clips and a headband; a bin; a laundry bin
You must never leave the client to fetch things.

ul: Wash your hands with soap and water, and dry them well, before and after every client. Warm hands are a pleasure; cold hands make the client flinch.
Keep your nails short, smooth and clean. Long nails scratch the skin and make it impossible to use finger pads properly.
Take off rings, bracelets and watches. They scratch the client, catch her hair and trap dirt.
Tie your hair back. Wear a clean uniform and flat, closed, comfortable shoes.
Keep your breath fresh and avoid strong perfume, which some clients react to.
Cover any cut on your hands with a waterproof plaster. If you have a skin infection, a cold or a fever, you do not give massages.
Greet her warmly, introduce yourself and take her to the private area.
Explain what the massage involves, how long it takes and what pressure she can expect. Tell her to say at once if anything hurts or she is uncomfortable.
Ask her to take off earrings, necklaces, glasses and hair clips, and to put them somewhere safe. They get in the way and could be damaged or hurt her.
Ask her to loosen or remove her top and wear a gown if oil will be used, or to keep her clothes on for a dry massage. Cover her with a towel for warmth and modesty.
Ask whether she needs the toilet before you begin.
She sits **upright**, with her back supported, her feet flat on the floor and her arms relaxed in her lap or on a pillow.
Her head should be level and in line with her spine, not pushed forward. If she prefers, she may lean forward onto a folded towel or pillow on a table, as long as she is comfortable.
Adjust the chair, pillows or your own position until she says she is comfortable. Do this before you start, not halfway through.

blocks.note: Never start with a client sitting in an unsafe place such as a swivel stool with no back. If she feels faint she could fall.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: You use your body all day, so you must work safely, or you will end up with a sore back, neck or thumbs.

ul: Stand with your feet apart, one slightly in front of the other, knees soft (not locked) and back straight.
Move your feet to follow your hands instead of twisting your back.
Lean in from your legs and use your **body weight** to make pressure. Do not push with your thumbs alone: that damages the thumb joints.
Change between thumbs, finger pads, the heel of the hand and the forearm (the forearm only if you have been trained).
Keep your shoulders relaxed and down; breathe normally.
Between clients, shake out your hands and wrists and stretch your neck and shoulders. Drink water and take your planned breaks.

blocks.note: In Jamaica many clients have tight necks and shoulders from long hours: route taxi drivers hold the wheel, call-centre agents wear headsets, office workers sit at screens, and vendors carry heavy loads. Ask each client about her work. It tells you where to spend time and which muscles are likely to be tight.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: The bones, muscles and vessels you work over

blocks.p: You cannot massage safely unless you know what lies under your hands. Learn these structures and where they are.

head: Bone
Where it is
rows: Cranium
The part of the skull round the brain. It is made of **8 bones**: one frontal, two parietal, two temporal, one occipital, one sphenoid and one ethmoid (the last two are deep inside).
Frontal bone
The forehead.
Parietal bones (a pair)
The top and upper sides of the skull.
Temporal bones (a pair)
The sides of the head, above and around the ears.
Occipital bone
The back and base of the skull. Many neck muscles join onto it.
Cervical vertebrae
The 7 small bones of the neck, from the base of the skull to the shoulders. The seventh sticks out at the base of the neck and is easy to feel.
Clavicle (collarbone)
Runs from the breastbone to the point of the shoulder, at the front.
Scapula (shoulder blade)
The flat, triangular bone at the back of the shoulder. It has a ridge (the spine of the scapula) you can feel.
Humerus
The long bone of the upper arm; its top forms the shoulder joint.

blocks.p: The 14 bones of the face are also part of the skull, but the massage works mainly on the scalp, forehead and temples.

head: Muscle
Where it is
What it does
What to know when massaging
rows: Frontalis
Across the forehead
Raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead
Light strokes and circles; often tight with worry and headaches.
Occipitalis
Back of the head
Pulls the scalp backwards
Joined to the frontalis by a tough sheet over the top of the head, so the scalp moves as one.
Temporalis
Fan-shaped, at the side of the head over the temple
Helps close the jaw when chewing
Clenching and grinding the teeth make it tight. Use small gentle circles.
Masseter
The cheek, at the angle of the jaw
Closes the jaw
Tight in people who clench their teeth.
Sternocleidomastoid
Each side of the neck, from behind the ear to the collarbone and breastbone
Turns and tilts the head
Work it gently with light kneading. Large blood vessels lie beside it.
Trapezius
A large diamond-shaped muscle over the back of the neck, the tops of the shoulders and the upper back
Lifts and pulls back the shoulders; helps hold the head up
The muscle most often tight and knotted. Most of your kneading and friction happens here.
Levator scapulae
Down the side of the back of the neck to the top of the shoulder blade
Lifts the shoulder blade
Often the cause of a 'stiff neck' after poor posture or a draught.
Deltoid
Rounded cap over the shoulder joint
Lifts the arm to the side and forward
Knead the top of the shoulder gently.

blocks.h: Blood vessels, lymph and other structures

ul: **Carotid arteries** run up the front and sides of the neck. They carry blood from the heart to the head. You can feel a pulse there. The **jugular veins** run beside them and bring blood back.

Pressure on the front and sides of the neck can press on these vessels and on the windpipe. It can make a client feel faint or frightened. The **thyroid gland** also lies at the front of the neck. So you never press or squeeze the **front and sides of the throat**.

**Lymph** is a clear fluid that carries waste and germs away from the tissues. It travels in thin vessels, much closer to the surface than the arteries, and passes through small bean-shaped **lymph nodes** (sometimes called glands). Nodes lie under the jaw, behind the ears, at the base of the skull and in the neck. The lymph drains downwards to the base of the neck, above the collarbones. Light, slow strokes towards the collarbone help the lymph to drain.
The **spine** runs down the middle of the back of the neck and back. It protects the spinal cord. You work on the muscles on either side of it, never directly on the bones.
Skin over bone, such as the spine, the collarbone, the shoulder blade ridge and the bone behind the ear, has little padding. It is easily bruised by hard pressure or striking movements.

blocks.note: Do not press hard on swollen or tender lymph nodes. Swollen nodes may mean the client is fighting an infection. Do not massage; suggest she sees her doctor.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: What massage does for the body and the mind

blocks.p: When you explain the massage to a client, and when you answer essay questions, you need to say clearly what massage does and does not do.

head: Effect
How it happens
rows: More blood flow to the area
Rubbing and kneading widen the small blood vessels near the skin and move blood through the muscle. More oxygen and food reach the cells, and the skin looks pinker and feels warmer.
Looser, less tense muscles
Warmth and kneading relax tight muscles and ease stiffness and muscle knots. This can help tension headaches that start in the neck and shoulders.
Better lymph flow
The pressure and rhythm help lymph carry waste away from the tissues, which can reduce puffiness.
Healthier scalp and skin
Scalp massage brings blood to the hair follicles and loosens dead skin. A medium softens the skin.
Calmer nerves and mind
Slow, steady, rhythmic movements soothe the nervous system. The client breathes more slowly, feels calmer, and may sleep better and feel less stress.
Awareness of the body
Many clients notice for the first time how tight their shoulders are, and learn to relax them.

blocks.note: Massage does not cure disease, make hair grow back, melt fat or replace a doctor. Never promise a cure. Say what it does: it relaxes, loosens muscles and helps circulation.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A knot (also called a trigger point) is a tight, tender lump in a muscle, often at the top of the shoulders. Slow kneading and small circles, with the client's agreement on pressure, can ease it. Never dig into a knot hard enough to cause sharp pain.

The consultation is a private conversation before you start. You find out what she wants, check that massage is safe for her, agree a plan and record it. Do it with her fully clothed and seated, in good light.

flow: Greet her and explain the service
Ask your questions
Look at the skin of the head, neck and shoulders
Check for contra-indications and allergies
Agree the plan, pressure and medium
She signs the form

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: What she wants and which areas bother her
Tells you where to spend time and what pressure she expects.
Her job and daily posture
Shows where tension is likely: driving, headsets, screens, carrying loads.
General health: blood pressure, heart, epilepsy, diabetes, bone problems, cancer treatment
Some conditions need her doctor's approval before any massage.
Injuries, operations and pain in the head, neck or shoulders
A recent injury can be made worse. Whiplash and sprains need a doctor.
Medicines, especially blood thinners
She may bruise easily, so the pressure must be light.
Allergies to oils, nuts, creams or perfume
So you can choose a safe medium. Read labels.
Pregnancy
She may need her doctor's approval, comfort cushions and a shorter time.
Headaches or migraines today; food and drink
A client with a migraine or who has just eaten a heavy meal will feel worse.
How much pressure she likes
Pressure is personal. Start light and adjust.

blocks.p: Look at the scalp, forehead, neck and shoulders. Look for cuts, grazes, bruises, swelling, rashes, boils, sunburn, scars, flaky patches, anything that looks infected, and moles or lumps that look changed. Touch only with clean hands and the pads of your fingers.
A **contra-indication** is a condition that means the massage must not go ahead, or must be changed. There are three groups.

head: Group
Examples
What you do
rows: Total: do not massage
Fever or high temperature
Infectious conditions: cold or flu, ringworm, impetigo, head lice, scabies
Recent injury such as whiplash, a sprain, a broken bone or a dislocation
A blood clot (thrombosis)
Swollen, tender lymph nodes
A client who has drunk alcohol, or just eaten a large meal
Explain kindly and privately. Do not diagnose. Suggest she rests or sees her doctor. Offer to rebook. Record it.
Local: avoid the area
Cuts, grazes, bruises and swelling
Sunburn
A boil or a rash
A recent scar or stitches
Broken or inflamed skin
Work only on healthy skin, with no pressure near the area. If the problem covers most of the area (for example sunburn across both shoulders), rebook.
Medical approval needed
High or low blood pressure; heart problems
Epilepsy; diabetes
Bone thinning (osteoporosis); a neck or spine problem
Cancer or its treatment; recent operation
Pregnancy
Do not go ahead until she has her doctor's approval. Follow any advice she is given. Offer to rebook.

blocks.note: If you are not sure whether to go ahead, do not. Ask your instructor or supervisor, and let the client check with her doctor. It is always better to rebook than to risk harm.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Never tell a client she has a disease. Describe what you see ('there is a swollen red area here'), explain that you cannot massage it, and suggest she sees a doctor or pharmacist. Do it quietly and in private.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: The client reads and signs the consultation form to show she has given true health details and agrees to the treatment. A client under 18 needs a parent or guardian to sign.
Write down any contra-indication found, and what you decided.

The form is personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act it must be kept private and secure, in a locked drawer or a password-protected system. Never discuss a client's health with other people.

blocks.p: A **contra-action** is an unwanted reaction during or after the treatment, such as dizziness, a headache, redness that does not fade, itching or a rash from the medium. Know how to deal with them (see 'Finishing, aftercare and records').
A **medium** is the oil, cream or powder that lets your hands glide over the skin without dragging. Some clients are massaged without a medium.

head: Medium
Best for
Take care
rows: Oil
Dry or normal skin; a smooth, long glide.
Some oils come from nuts (almond is common). Ask about allergies. Oil can stain clothes and leave hair greasy.
Cream or lotion
Normal skin; soaks in more than oil.
Take it from the tub with a clean spatula; never dip your fingers in.
Powder (talc)
Oily or sweaty skin; gives light glide.
It makes dust and can irritate the lungs. Do not use it near a client with asthma.
No medium (dry massage)
Over clothing at a workplace or event; clients with allergies; clients who do not want oil.
Use firmer, slower strokes through the cloth and take care not to drag on the skin or pinch it.
Essential oils
Only if you have been trained.
Never use undiluted. Many cause reactions. Ask about allergies first.

blocks.h: Choosing and using a medium safely

ul: Ask about allergies at the consultation. If the client is unsure, do a small test on a patch of skin before the massage, following the maker's instructions.
Read the label and follow the maker's instructions.

Pour a small amount into a **clean bowl for this client only**, or lift cream out with a **clean spatula**. Never dip your used fingers back into the main bottle or tub. It puts germs into the product.
Warm the medium in your hands first. Cold oil makes the client jump.
Use just enough for your hands to glide. Too much makes your hands slip and leaves the client messy; too little drags the skin.
Keep oil away from the eyes and the hairline. For the scalp, use very little or none; ask first, especially if her hair is relaxed, in braids or locs, or freshly styled.
Afterwards wipe off the extra with a tissue or warm towel, close the bottle, store it in a cool, dark place, and wash the bowl and spatula.

blocks.note: Jamaica's heat makes oils and creams go rancid or separate faster. Keep them out of the sun, away from windows and hot equipment, and check the smell and look before use.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: The massage movements and how to use them

blocks.p: Each movement has a name, a way of doing it and a reason for using it. A good massage links them smoothly in an order.

head: Movement
How you do it
Effect
Where and when
rows: Effleurage

Smooth, gliding strokes with the palms or finger pads. Light for spreading and finishing; firmer for warming. Move in the direction of the lymph and the heart: down the back of the neck and out over the shoulders.
Relaxes; warms the skin; spreads the medium; helps lymph; lets the client get used to your touch.
Start and end the massage; link the other movements; between them.
Petrissage (kneading)
Press, lift and squeeze the muscle with the palm, or the thumb and fingers, then release. Includes kneading, picking up, rolling and wringing.
Loosens tight muscle; moves waste out and fresh blood in.
Tops of the shoulders and the trapezius; upper arms.
Friction
Small, deep circles with the thumbs or finger pads. The skin moves over the muscle beneath; your fingers do not slide.
Warms and loosens small areas; eases knots.
Either side of the spine, along the top of the shoulder blades, at the base of the skull, and on the scalp.
Tapotement (percussion)
Quick, light, springy striking: hacking (sides of the hands), cupping (hollow hands), pounding (loose fists) and tapping (fingertips). Wrists are loose.
Stimulates the skin, nerves and muscles.
Only on thick, fleshy areas such as the tops of the shoulders. Short and light.
Vibration
A fine, fast trembling movement made with the finger pads or the hands.
Stimulates; can relax a tense spot.
Short bursts on the scalp, at the temples or on the shoulders.

blocks.note: Never use tapotement over bone, such as the spine, the collarbones or the shoulder blade ridge. Do not use it on bruised, sore or thin skin, on older clients, on a client with a headache, or on the neck or throat.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Pressure**: start light, build up slowly, and ask 'Is that all right for you?' Adjust to the client. A feeling that eases as you work is fine; sharp pain, pins and needles or numbness are not. Stop and ask.
**Rhythm**: keep a steady, even pace. Sudden changes make the client tense up.
**Speed**: slow movements relax; quick ones stimulate. A relaxing massage is mostly slow.
**Contact**: keep at least one hand on the client wherever you can, so the massage feels continuous. When you must lift both hands, do it slowly and lightly, and say so.
**Direction**: heavier strokes go towards the heart and the nodes at the base of the neck; lighter strokes come back.
**Smoothness**: finish each movement properly and glide into the next one.

blocks.note: Work on the muscles beside the spine, never on the spine. Never press the throat. Never twist, pull, click or crack the neck or head: that is joint manipulation, which needs a different training, and it can cause serious injury.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Giving a seated head, neck and shoulder massage

blocks.p: A full seated massage takes about 20 to 30 minutes. Use the plan below as a guide. Always follow the consultation and the client's comfort, and the Centre's routine.

flow: Rest your hands lightly on her shoulders
Warm and apply the medium with effleurage over the upper back and shoulders
Petrissage on the shoulders and trapezius
Friction beside the spine and along the shoulder blades
Effleurage to link
Neck: gentle kneading and finger circles at the back
Scalp: finger-pad circles and vibration
Forehead and temples: light stroking
Slow closing effleurage; rest hands still

head: Stage
What you do
Typical time
rows: 1. Settle
Hands resting on shoulders; a moment of stillness; tell her you are starting.
1 minute
2. Warm and spread
Effleurage on the upper back, shoulders and neck.
3 minutes
3. Shoulders
Petrissage on the trapezius and tops of the shoulders, then the upper arms; light tapotement if suitable.
5 minutes
4. Knots
Friction with the thumbs beside the spine and along the shoulder blades; effleurage between.
4 minutes
5. Neck
Gentle kneading and finger circles on the back and sides of the neck; support the head with one hand. Never the throat.
3 minutes
6. Scalp
Finger-pad circles over the whole scalp: hairline to crown to nape; light vibration; gentle hair lifts only if the client likes them.
6 minutes
7. Face edges
Light stroking over the forehead and temples; small circles at the temples.
2 minutes
8. Finish
Slow effleurage, then hands resting still; tell her quietly it is over.
1 minute

blocks.p: These add up to 25 minutes. Stage times are a guide and change with the client. Add time to the booking for the consultation, for helping her sit up and drink water, and for writing the record.

ul: Use the **pads** of the fingers, never the nails.
Place the fingers firmly on the scalp and move the scalp itself over the bone in small circles, rather than sliding over the hair.
Work from the front hairline to the crown, over the sides, behind the ears and down to the nape.
Pressure is firm but never pulling. Keep the pace slow.

head: Client
What you change
rows: Very tense shoulders
Warm the area longer with effleurage. Build up slowly with slow petrissage and friction on the trapezius and shoulder blades. Ask often. Never press so hard that it hurts.
Older client or thin, fragile skin
Lighter pressure; a little more medium so the skin is not dragged; no tapotement; check her neck and comfort often; allow her extra time to stand.
Client who bruises easily or takes blood thinners
Light pressure only; no deep friction or pinching; ask her doctor if unsure.
Braids, locs or extensions
Ask whether she wants oil on the scalp. Work with finger pads on the parts between braids; press and circle, do not rub or pull. Locs: no oil or wax; do not drag.
Relaxed or freshly styled hair
Little or no medium on the scalp; light movements.
Headache or migraine
Do not massage if the headache is severe or sudden. For mild tension, use very light, slow work.
Massage over clothing at an event
No medium. Ask her to remove necklaces and clips. Use slower, firmer strokes through the cloth. 15 minutes is usual.

blocks.note: If at any time the client says she feels dizzy, sick, has pins and needles, numbness, sharp pain or difficulty breathing, **stop**. Keep her seated, give her water, stay with her and call a supervisor. If she does not recover quickly, get medical help.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: At an event or workplace wellness day, clean the chair and face rest and change the cover between every client. Allow a short gap between clients to do this. Agree the number of clients and the finishing time with the organiser first.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Finish with slow effleurage and rest your hands still
Tell her quietly that the massage is over
Let her sit for a moment with her eyes closed
Help her sit up slowly; give her water
Ask how she feels, and about the pressure
Give aftercare advice
Help her put on her things; make a next appointment if she wishes

blocks.p: Some clients feel light-headed when they move quickly after deep relaxation. Never hurry her. Stay with her until she is steady.

ul: Drink plenty of water for the rest of the day.
Rest if you can. Avoid stress, hard exercise, heavy meals and alcohol for a few hours.
If oil is left in the hair, wash it later with warm (not very hot) water.
Keep shoulders warm. Do not sit in a strong draught.
Good posture, regular breaks and gentle stretching help the benefits last. Book again when she needs it.

head: Reaction
Is it normal?
What she should do
rows: Feeling tired or sleepy
Yes, often
Rest.
A little light-headed when standing
Yes, mild; passes quickly
Sit and drink water. Stand slowly.
Slight soreness in worked muscles; a mild headache
Yes, mild; passes within a day
Rest, drink water, keep warm.
Needing to pass urine more often; feeling emotional
Yes
Drink water. It passes.
Redness that spreads, itching or a rash where the medium was used
No: a contra-action
Wash it off; stop using that product; contact the salon; see a doctor if it does not settle.
Strong dizziness, nausea, severe pain or a reaction lasting more than a day or two
No
Contact the salon and see a doctor.

blocks.note: Record any contra-action on her record card and tell your supervisor. If there was an injury or accident, write it in the accident book.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Put used towels and gowns in the closed laundry bin
Wipe the chair and face rest with disinfectant, for the contact time on the label
Wash the bowl and spatula; throw away used tissues
Close and store the medium in a cool, dark place
Wash and dry your hands
Reset the area for the next client

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, client's name and contact details
11/11/2026, Winston Grant, Half-Way Tree
Health details and contra-indications
Tension in the neck; no contra-indications; doctor's approval seen for blood pressure
Medium used
Nut-free cream
Areas worked and the movements used
Shoulders, neck and scalp: effleurage, petrissage, friction
Pressure and the client's response
Medium; she said it was just right
Contra-actions
None
Aftercare advice and next appointment
Water, rest; return in 2 weeks
Signed form and the therapist's name
Signed; K. Allen (trainee), checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Client records are personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they must be kept private and secure. Only the staff who need them should see them.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can prepare the room, my own body and the client for a seated massage.
I can sit the client safely and protect my own posture.
I can name the main bones of the head, neck and shoulder and say where they are.
I can name the main muscles, say where each is and what it does.
I can explain why I never press the front or sides of the throat or the spine.
I can explain how massage helps the blood, the lymph, the muscles and the mind.
I can carry out a consultation and explain why each question matters.
I can sort a client's condition into: massage, adapt, or refer, and give my reason.
I can explain consent, the consultation form and why it is kept private.
I can choose and use a medium hygienically, and check for allergies.
I can do effleurage, petrissage, friction, tapotement and vibration, and say where each is used and not used.
I can control pressure, rhythm, speed and contact.
I can put the movements together into a 20 to 30 minute routine.
I can adapt the massage for tense shoulders, thin skin, braids, locs and massage over clothing.
I can recognise a contra-action and deal with it.
I can give aftercare advice, clean up and complete the record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give a reason for each step. For example: 'I ask about nut allergies, because some oils are made from nuts and could cause a reaction.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The oil, cream or powder that helps the hands glide.
Smooth, gliding strokes; used to start, link and finish.
Kneading: pressing, lifting and squeezing the muscle.
Small, deep circles with the thumbs or finger pads.
Quick, light striking: hacking, cupping, pounding, tapping.
The bone of the upper arm.
The bone at the back and base of the skull.
Large muscle over the back of the neck, shoulders and upper back.
Muscle on each side of the neck that turns the head.
Muscle at the back of the head.
Fan-shaped muscle at the side of the head.
Muscle over the shoulder joint that lifts the arm.
Main arteries up the front and sides of the neck.
Clear fluid that carries waste away from the tissues.
Small structures along lymph vessels that filter the lymph.
A condition that stops the massage or means it must be changed.
An unwanted reaction during or after a treatment.
A blood clot in a vein; a contra-indication.
The signed form showing the client has given her health details and agrees to the massage.
A tight, tender lump in a muscle.
The client's record of consultation, treatment, advice and reactions.

c1.title: A route taxi driver in Half-Way Tree
c1.text: Mr. Winston Grant, 52, drives a route taxi ten hours a day and books a massage for his stiff neck and tight shoulders. During the consultation he tells trainee Kimberly that he takes tablets for high blood pressure, but he has not seen his doctor for about six months. He says he is keen to start because he has a free hour now.

c2.title: Braids and a nut allergy in Portmore
c2.text: Shanice Williams, 29, works in a call centre and wears a headset all day. Her knotless box braids are six weeks old. She asks for a massage with oil, but tells trainee Dwayne that almonds make her lips swell. The salon has almond-based massage oil, a nut-free cream in a tub, and a spatula.

c3.title: An older client in May Pen
c3.text: Miss Icilda Barnes, 72, has thin skin and says she bruises easily because she takes blood-thinning tablets. Her doctor has told her she has some bone thinning. Her neck is stiff, and she says she gets dizzy if she stands up too fast.

c4.title: A wellness day at a Kingston office
c4.text: A company in Kingston has booked the Centre's trainees for a wellness day. Chair massage over clothing runs from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. Each client has a 15-minute massage, and a 5-minute gap follows each one for cleaning and reset. The trainees use a massage chair with a face rest. No oil may be used.

c5.title: Sunburn and a lump at the hairline
c5.text: Ms. Natalie Brown comes for a seated massage after a weekend at the beach. Her shoulders and upper back are red, hot and tender from sunburn. She also has a painful red lump with a yellow tip near her hairline at the back of her neck. She asks trainee Aisha, 'Can you tell me what it is?'

questions.q: What should Kimberly do about Mr. Grant's blood pressure?
o: Go ahead, but use only the lightest pressure for the whole massage
Go ahead, but leave out the neck and work only on his shoulders
Say she needs his doctor's approval first, and offer to rebook
Check his blood pressure with the salon's machine and then decide
questions.why: High blood pressure needs a doctor's approval before massage. A massage therapist does not decide this herself, and light pressure or leaving out the neck does not remove the risk.

questions.q: Why are Mr. Grant's neck and shoulder muscles so tight?
o: Holding one position for hours keeps them tense and cuts blood flow
His tablets for blood pressure make the muscles shorter and harder
His seat is too warm, which makes the muscles swell and then stiffen
The bones of his neck have slowly grown closer together over the years
questions.why: Muscles held in one position for hours stay contracted, tire, and get less fresh blood, so tension and knots build up. Massage helps by warming the muscle and improving the blood flow.

questions.q: His doctor now says he may have a massage. How should Kimberly start with the pressure?
o: Whatever pressure he asks for, and no questions after the first minute
Medium pressure straight away, because tight muscles need strong work
Very light pressure only, for as long as the massage lasts
Start light, build up slowly and keep asking him how it feels
questions.why: Pressure is always built up gradually and checked with the client. Strong work on cold muscles hurts, and constant light pressure will not ease knots; the client's comfort decides.

questions.q: What is the safest choice of medium for Shanice?
o: The almond oil, as only a small amount touches her skin
A dry massage or the nut-free cream, once she has read the label
A different oil from another bottle, because she is only allergic to almonds
The almond oil, after she has washed her hands to remove any nut traces
questions.why: A client with a nut allergy must not be given a nut-based product. Offer a dry massage, or a cream she has checked, and do not guess about other oils.

questions.q: How should Dwayne take the cream from the tub?
o: By tipping the tub and shaking some out
With a clean spatula, for this client only
With the spatula, which he then returns to the tub
With clean fingers, then wipe them on a tissue
questions.why: A clean spatula keeps fingers out of the tub, so germs do not get into the product. A spatula that has been used on the client must not go back in.

questions.q: How should Dwayne work on Shanice's scalp, given her braids?
o: Leave out the scalp completely, as it cannot be reached through braids
Rub the length of each braid firmly to loosen the scalp underneath
Lift the braids in bunches and pull them gently to stretch the scalp
Finger-pad circles on the partings between braids, with no pulling
questions.why: The scalp can be reached along the partings. Pressing and circling with the finger pads works without loosening the braids; rubbing or pulling frizzes them and hurts the roots.

questions.q: Why would a headset worn all day leave Shanice with a tight neck?
o: The same muscles hold the head tilted for hours and become tight
The headset presses on the carotid arteries and cuts off the blood
The neck bones are slowly pushed together by the weight of the headset
Wearing a headset all day makes the neck muscles grow weak and loose
questions.why: Holding the head to one side or forward for hours keeps the same neck and shoulder muscles contracted. Asking about a client's work tells you where to look for tension.

questions.q: Miss Barnes bruises easily. How should Trainee Camille adjust the massage?
o: Firm pressure with short strokes, to keep the skin from dragging
Light pressure, but with hacking to keep the blood moving in her skin
Light pressure, no pinching or deep friction, and plenty of medium
Normal pressure, since bruises show only if the client is being hurt
questions.why: Thin, fragile skin and blood thinners mean she bruises easily. Gentle pressure, good glide and no striking or pinching protect her skin; tapotement can bruise.

questions.q: Miss Barnes has been told she has bone thinning. Which action is best?
o: Press more firmly on the spine, so that she feels the muscles working
Treat her like any other client, since her doctor has not banned massage
Skip the shoulders and work only on her scalp for the whole session
Check with her doctor, keep pressure light and stay off the spine
questions.why: Bone thinning can make bones fragile, so ask her doctor and keep pressure light. The spine is never pressed in any client, and a doctor should say what is safe.

questions.q: At the end Miss Barnes says she is dizzy when she stands. What should Camille do?
o: Give her water and help her up slowly once she feels steady
Help her up quickly so that the blood returns to her head
Tell her to walk around at once to clear her head
Ask her to sit up straight and wait without saying anything to her
questions.why: Quick movements after deep relaxation can make a client light-headed. Let her sit, give water, ask how she feels and help her stand slowly.

questions.q: How many clients can the trainees massage between 10:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. on one chair?
questions.why: Each client uses 15 minutes plus a 5-minute gap, which is 20 minutes. Three hours is 180 minutes, and 180 divided by 20 is 9.

questions.q: Why must no oil be used on this wellness day?
o: It makes the muscles too relaxed for people who must work afterwards
Oil would stain their clothes and could cause reactions at work
Therapists' hands cannot hold oil while they work through cloth
Oil blocks the face rest on a massage chair and cannot be cleaned off
questions.why: A seated massage over clothing is dry. Oil would soak into clothes and could trigger reactions, and clients return to work straight away.

questions.q: What must the trainees do with the face rest between clients?
o: Wipe it with disinfectant and put on a fresh cover
Turn it over so that the clean side is used by the next client
Leave it until the end of the day, when everything is cleaned together
Spray it with perfume to hide the smell of the last client
questions.why: Anything that touches a client's face must be cleaned between clients to prevent the spread of germs; a quick turn or a perfume does not do this.

questions.q: What should Aisha do about Natalie's sunburn?
o: Use cool oil and very light strokes over the burnt skin
Massage the burnt areas with the palms only, without any pressure
Do not massage, and offer to rebook once the skin has healed
Massage only the unburnt areas and use more oil on the burnt areas
questions.why: Sunburn is a local contra-indication. Because it covers both shoulders and the upper back, there is no healthy skin left to work on, so she should rebook.

questions.q: What should Aisha do about the lump with the yellow tip at the hairline?
o: Work gently over it, using only a very small amount of cream
Avoid the area, explain why, and suggest she sees a doctor
Squeeze it gently to let out the pus before she begins the massage
Cover it with a plaster and carry on working all around the plaster
questions.why: A boil or infected spot is a contra-indication: pressure could spread the infection and hurts. Aisha does not treat it. She describes what she sees and suggests a doctor.

questions.q: How should Aisha answer 'Can you tell me what it is?'
o: Tell her it is a boil, because it is red and has a yellow tip on it
Say it is probably only an insect bite and will go away on its own
Say nothing about it and just rebook her, so as not to worry her
Say she cannot diagnose it, describe it, and advise a doctor
questions.why: Therapists do not diagnose. Describe what you see calmly and privately, explain why you cannot massage the area and advise her to see a doctor.

questions.q: Halfway through a different client's massage, she says her hand feels numb and tingly. What is the best response?
o: Move to the scalp, which will take her mind off her arm
Tell her this is normal and will pass as the muscle warms up
Stop, ask her how she feels, keep her seated and call the supervisor
Press more softly but carry on with the same movement for another minute
questions.why: Pins and needles or numbness may mean a nerve is being pressed. Stop at once, check on her and get help if it does not pass.

questions.q: A client's massage starts at 2:50 p.m. and lasts 30 minutes. She then needs 10 minutes for water, advice and paperwork. When is the chair free to start cleaning for the next client?
questions.why: 2:50 p.m. plus 30 minutes is 3:20 p.m., and 10 more minutes make 3:30 p.m. Cleaning then starts, and the next client must be booked after it.

questions.q: In which direction should effleurage strokes on the neck and shoulders mostly go?
o: Up from the shoulders to the scalp, to bring blood to the head
Across the throat from side to side, to relax the neck muscles
Up and down along the spine, from the lower back to the neck
Down towards the collarbones, helping the lymph to drain
questions.why: Lymph drains to the nodes at the base of the neck above the collarbones, and heavier strokes go towards the heart. Strokes must never cross the throat or press the spine.

questions.q: A trainee therapist gets sore thumbs after five massages in a row. Which change would help her most?
o: Use body weight from her legs and change between thumbs and palms
Stand further from the client to keep her wrists perfectly straight
Use a much thinner oil so that her thumbs slip over the muscle faster
Press harder with her thumbs so that each massage can be shorter
questions.why: Pressing with the thumbs alone strains the joints. Using body weight from the legs, changing between thumbs, finger pads and palms, and taking breaks protect the therapist.
